AMD's FY2025 10-K specifically names its key foundry suppliers and their respective process-node responsibilities, stating that it relies on TSMC "for the production of all wafers for microprocessor and GPU products at 7 nanometer (nm) or smaller nodes" and "primarily on GLOBALFOUNDRIES Inc. (GF) for wafers for microprocessor and GPU products manufactured at process nodes larger than 7 nm [1]." AMD also uses TSMC, UMC, and Samsung for integrated circuits in programmable logic devices, relies on third-party manufacturers for assembly, test, mark and pack operations, and notes it lacks long-term commitment contracts with some suppliers, obtaining many of those services on a purchase order basis with no guaranteed minimum quantities beyond existing orders [1]. AMD's filing reinforces that TSMC concentration by warning that if TSMC is unable to manufacture wafers at 7 nm or smaller nodes in sufficient quantities to meet customer demand, it could have a material adverse effect on AMD's business [2].

NVIDIA's FY2026 10-K groups foundry and packaging concentration into a bulleted enumeration of supply-chain risks, including one entry described as "limited number and geographic concentration of global suppliers, foundries, contract manufacturers, assembly and test providers and memory manufacturers [3]." NVIDIA's list also covers lack of guaranteed supply, potential higher wafer prices from inaccurate demand estimates, low manufacturing yields, complexity from integrating new suppliers, and the risk that foundries prioritize competitors' or other customers' orders over NVIDIA's [3]. NVIDIA notes that it does not assemble, test, or package its products itself, but instead contracts with independent subcontractors, and groups assembly and packaging concentration risk within that same supply-chain bullet framework [3].

Intel's FY2025 10-K describes foundry concentration from two directions: Intel already uses TSMC for certain components of its current products, and faces the prospect of far greater TSMC dependence if its own foundry strategy fails [4][5]. Intel states that if it pauses Intel 14A development, its products business would become "dependent on third-party foundries, particularly TSMC," noting it has no long-term contract with TSMC while most competitors have longer and more established relationships with that foundry [4]. Intel notes that leading-edge foundry capacity is limited to "currently only TSMC and Samsung," and that some of its most advanced current and future products are already "exclusively manufactured by TSMC or reliant upon critical components, including various compute die, manufactured by TSMC [4][5]."

Intel's FY2025 advanced-packaging disclosure is the most architecturally specific of the three filings' passages, describing a disaggregated tile design in which components manufactured on different processes are joined by advanced packaging technologies, "several of which are novel, have a limited manufacturing history or have increased costs [6]." Intel further warns that any interruption in the supply of TSMC-manufactured tiles would prevent completing products until replacement tiles could be designed and sourced from an alternative supplier, an effort that "would likely involve a substantial delay given the bespoke design of each tile to the particular manufacturing process utilized [6]." AMD's FY2025 filing addresses packaging risk at a higher level, noting that third-party package assembly partners are responsible for packaging technology and that during periods when manufacturers implement new process or packaging technologies, their facilities may not be fully productive [1][2].
